docs.title: 5. Building Your First Yoriito Vehicle API Application 📱
5-1. Introduction
docs.text: In this tutorial, you will learn how to use the Yoriito Signal API through sample code, and build a sample application with it. By running the development environment you built in Chapter 4, you can experience application development using the Yoriito Signal API.

docs.title: 5-2. Basics
docs.text:
The Yoriito Signal API is a set of APIs that correspond one-to-one with Yoriito VSS. It consists of:

  1. Get – to obtain the current value
  2. Set – to set a target value
  3. Subscribe – to continuously receive changes in the current value

This section shows sample code for each of these.

For more details on the Yoriito Signal API, see "2. System Configuration/Scope/Versioning". For more details on VSS, see "3. VSS/VISS".

Try running and modifying the sample code, and apply it to your own application development. To check the behavior of the sample code, make sure to start the simulator first by following "4-6. Start the simulator".

docs.title: 5-2-1. Check the current state of the high beam: Get
docs.text:
What is Get?

  • Get is used when you want to obtain the current value.
  • You can call Get for signals whose type is Actuator / Sensor / Attribute.

Sample code (yoriito-tutorial/tutorial/get/src/main.cc)

  • The following code retrieves the current high-beam state (ON/OFF).
#include "yoriito/yoriito_log.h"
#include <yoriito/signal/body/Body.h>

namespace {
constexpr int kExitOk = 0;
constexpr int kExitNg = 1;
} // namespace

int main() {
  YORIITO_LOG_INITIALIZE("get");

  auto result = yoriito::vehicle::body::lights::beam::high::ison::Get();

  if (result.IsErr()) {
    auto err = result.TakeErr();
    YORIITO_LOG_ERROR("get", std::string("Get failed: ") + err->Message() +
                                 " (code=" + std::to_string(err->ErrorCode()) +
                                 ")");
    YORIITO_LOG_FINALIZE();
    return kExitNg;
  }

  auto data_point = result.TakeOk().value();
  const bool value = data_point.GetData();

  YORIITO_LOG_INFO("get",
                   std::string("Get succeeded: ") + (value ? "true" : "false"));

  YORIITO_LOG_FINALIZE();
  return kExitOk;
}

Build & run steps

  1. Start the simulator if it is not running yet.

    $ cd /work/ref_pal
$ npm ci
$ ./init_pal.sh
$ npx electron . --no-sandbox

  2. Build

    $ cd /work/tutorial/get
$ cmake -S . -B build
$ cmake --build build -j

  3. Run

    $ ./build/get

Info

If the command fails with a No data error, rerun ./init_pal.sh to initialize the signal data, then retry the command.

Example use cases

  • Display the current state on the screen
    • e.g., get "High beam: ON/OFF", "Wiper: AUTO" and reflect them in the UI
  • Get the current value only when needed
    • e.g., fetch values only when the user presses a "Refresh" button

docs.title: 5-2-2. Turn on the high beam: Set
docs.text:
What is Set?

  • Set is used when you want to set a target value.
  • You can call Set only for signals whose type is Actuator.

Sample code (yoriito-tutorial/tutorial/set/src/main.cc)

#include "yoriito/yoriito_log.h"
#include <yoriito/signal/body/Body.h>

namespace {
constexpr int kExitOk = 0;
constexpr int kExitNg = 1;
} // namespace

int main() {
  YORIITO_LOG_INITIALIZE("set");

  const bool is_on = true;
  yoriito::Result<void> set_result =
      yoriito::vehicle::body::lights::beam::high::ison::Set(is_on);

  if (set_result.IsErr()) {
    const yoriito::Result<void>::ErrorPtr err = set_result.TakeErr();
    YORIITO_LOG_ERROR("set", std::string("Set failed: ") + err->Message() +
                                 " (code=" + std::to_string(err->ErrorCode()) +
                                 ")");
    YORIITO_LOG_FINALIZE();
    return kExitNg;
  }

  YORIITO_LOG_INFO(
      "set", std::string("Set succeeded: ") + (is_on ? "true" : "false"));

  YORIITO_LOG_FINALIZE();
  return kExitOk;
}

Build & run steps

  1. Start the simulator if it is not running yet.

    $ cd /work/ref_pal
$ npm ci
$ ./init_pal.sh
$ npx electron . --no-sandbox

  2. Build

    $ cd /work/tutorial/set
$ cmake -S . -B build
$ cmake --build build -j

  3. Run

    $ ./build/set

Info

If the command fails with a No data error, rerun ./init_pal.sh to initialize the signal data, then retry the command.

Example use cases

  • Control vehicle functions based on user operations
    • e.g., high beam ON/OFF, A/C temperature setting, seat heater ON/OFF etc.

docs.title: 5-2-3. Receive a high-beam state change: Subscribe
docs.text:
What is Subscribe?

  • Subscribe is used when you want to continuously receive changes in the current value.
  • You can call Subscribe for signals whose type is Actuator / Sensor.
  • In this sample, the application waits for one high-beam state update, outputs the received value, and then calls UnSubscribe to end the subscription.

Sample code (yoriito-tutorial/tutorial/subscribe/src/main.cc)

#include "yoriito/yoriito_log.h"
#include <yoriito/signal/body/Body.h>

namespace {
constexpr int kExitOk = 0;
constexpr int kExitNg = 1;

namespace high_beam = yoriito::vehicle::body::lights::beam::high::ison;
} // namespace

int main() {
  YORIITO_LOG_INITIALIZE("subscribe");

  auto subscribe_result = high_beam::Subscribe();
  if (subscribe_result.IsErr()) {
    auto error = subscribe_result.TakeErr();
    YORIITO_LOG_ERROR("subscribe",
                      std::string("Subscribe failed: ") + error->Message() +
                          " (code=" + std::to_string(error->ErrorCode()) + ")");
    YORIITO_LOG_FINALIZE();
    return kExitNg;
  }

  auto subscription_context = subscribe_result.TakeOk().value();
  YORIITO_LOG_INFO("subscribe", "Waiting for one update...");

  int exit_code = kExitOk;

  auto message_result = subscription_context.Messages();
  if (message_result.IsErr()) {
    auto error = message_result.TakeErr();
    YORIITO_LOG_ERROR("subscribe",
                      std::string("Messages() failed: ") + error->Message() +
                          " (code=" + std::to_string(error->ErrorCode()) + ")");
    exit_code = kExitNg;
  } else {
    auto data_point = message_result.TakeOk().value();
    const bool is_on = data_point.GetData();

    YORIITO_LOG_INFO("subscribe", std::string("IsOn updated: ") +
                                      (is_on ? "true" : "false"));
  }

  auto unsubscribe_result =
      high_beam::UnSubscribe(std::move(subscription_context));
  if (unsubscribe_result.IsErr()) {
    auto error = unsubscribe_result.TakeErr();
    YORIITO_LOG_ERROR("subscribe",
                      std::string("UnSubscribe failed: ") + error->Message() +
                          " (code=" + std::to_string(error->ErrorCode()) + ")");
    exit_code = kExitNg;
  } else {
    YORIITO_LOG_INFO("subscribe", "UnSubscribe succeeded.");
  }

  YORIITO_LOG_FINALIZE();
  return exit_code;
}

Build & run steps

  1. Start the simulator if it is not running yet.

    $ cd /work/ref_pal
$ npm ci
$ ./init_pal.sh
$ npx electron . --no-sandbox

  2. Build

    $ cd /work/tutorial/subscribe
$ cmake -S . -B build
$ cmake --build build -j
# If not already done, build Set as well
$ cd /work/tutorial/set
$ cmake -S . -B build
$ cmake --build build -j

  3. Run

    • First, run Subscribe:

      $ cd /work/tutorial/subscribe
$ ./build/subscribe

    • Then, in another terminal, run Set:

      $ cd /work/tutorial/set
$ ./build/set

    • After Set runs, the Subscribe process receives one update, unsubscribes, and exits.

Info

If the command fails with a No data error, rerun ./init_pal.sh to initialize the signal data, then retry the command.

Example use cases

  • Reflect state changes in the UI in real time
    • e.g., when the physical high-beam switch changes ON/OFF, the app UI updates immediately
  • Detect abnormalities
    • e.g., show a warning if temperature exceeds a specified value

docs.title: 5-3. Advanced
docs.text: In the Basics section, you learned how to obtain and control vehicle signals using Get / Set / Subscribe of the Yoriito Signal API. In the Advanced section, you will learn concepts needed to develop more realistic applications, along with sample code.

docs.title: 5-3-1. Check whether the front fog light is available: Availability
docs.text:
What is Availability?

  • In the Basics section, sample code for Get / Set / Subscribe assumed that the high-beam signal is available.
  • In this section, the sample code checks the availability of the front fog light as both a sensor and an actuator.
  • In real vehicles, however, a signal may or may not be usable depending on the vehicle state and conditions. A function may be available on one vehicle but not on another.
  • To inform applications of these differences, Availability is provided to represent whether a signal is usable.
  • Availability takes either true or false:
    • true: the signal is currently available
    • false: the signal exists but is currently unavailable
  • Depending on the kind of signal, two types of Availability are defined:
    • Availability_Sensor
      • Indicates whether the current value can be obtained via Get.
    • Availability_Actuator
      • Indicates whether the target value can be set via Set.
  • For more details on Availability, see "2-5. System Behavior".

Sample code (yoriito-tutorial/tutorial/availability/src/main.cc)

#include "yoriito/yoriito_log.h"
#include <yoriito/signal/body/Body.h>

namespace {
constexpr int kExitOk = 0;
constexpr int kExitNg = 1;
} // namespace

int main() {
  YORIITO_LOG_INITIALIZE("availability");
  auto result = yoriito::vehicle::body::lights::fog::front::ison::Get();

  if (result.IsErr()) {
    auto err = result.TakeErr();
    YORIITO_LOG_ERROR("availability",
                      std::string("Get failed: ") + err->Message() +
                          " (code=" + std::to_string(err->ErrorCode()) + ")");
    YORIITO_LOG_FINALIZE();
    return kExitNg;
  }

  auto data_point = result.TakeOk().value();
  const bool is_available_sensor = data_point.IsAvailableSensor();
  const bool is_available_actuator = data_point.IsAvailableActuator();

  YORIITO_LOG_INFO("availability",
                   std::string("Available Sensor: ") +
                       (is_available_sensor ? "true" : "false"));
  YORIITO_LOG_INFO("availability",
                   std::string("Available Actuator: ") +
                       (is_available_actuator ? "true" : "false"));

  YORIITO_LOG_FINALIZE();
  return kExitOk;
}

Build & run steps

  1. Start the simulator if it is not running yet.

    $ cd /work/ref_pal
$ npm ci
$ ./init_pal.sh
$ npx electron . --no-sandbox

  2. Build

    $ cd /work/tutorial/availability
$ cmake -S . -B build
$ cmake --build build -j

  3. Run

    $ ./build/availability

Tip

Try changing the signal in the sample code to another one, then rebuild and run. For example, if you change it to yoriito::vehicle::body::lights::beam::high::ison, both sensor and actuator availability should be true.

Example use cases

Availability is mainly used in the following situations:

  • GUI control
    • Automatically gray out buttons for unavailable functions.
  • User guidance
    • Show messages such as "Currently not operable" when conditions are not met (e.g., while driving).
  • Check before sending operation requests
    • Verify availability before sending an operation request via the API.

This ensures the UI/application behavior stays consistent with the actual vehicle state.

docs.title: 5-3-2. Get detailed information (metadata) of the high beam: Inspect
docs.text:
What is Inspect?

  • In the Basics section, we dealt with Boolean signals. In real vehicles, there are also int and float signals.
  • In such cases, you may want to know the minimum and maximum values.
  • For example, for vehicle speed, you may want to know whether the unit is km/h or mph.
  • For this purpose, the Inspect method is provided.
  • By calling Inspect, you can get detailed information (metadata) of a signal.

  • Key data fields obtainable via Inspect:

    Data Meaning path Full path of the signal (e.g. Vehicle.Body.Lights.Beam.High.IsOn) datatype Data type (e.g. boolean, int, float, string) entry_type Node type: branch / sensor / actuator / attribute unit Unit (e.g. km/h, %, °C) min Minimum value max Maximum value comment Additional notes allowed Allowed values (e.g. ['AUTO', 'LOW', 'MID', 'HIGH']) default_value Default value description Description of the signal array_size Number of elements if it is an array

Sample code (yoriito-tutorial/tutorial/inspect/src/main.cc)

#include "yoriito/yoriito_log.h"
#include <yoriito/signal/body/Body.h>

namespace {
constexpr int kExitOk = 0;
constexpr int kExitNg = 1;
} // namespace

int main() {
  YORIITO_LOG_INITIALIZE("inspect");

  auto result = yoriito::vehicle::body::lights::beam::high::ison::Inspect();

  if (result.IsErr()) {
    auto err = result.TakeErr();
    YORIITO_LOG_ERROR("inspect",
                      std::string("Inspect failed: ") + err->Message() +
                          " (code=" + std::to_string(err->ErrorCode()) + ")");
    YORIITO_LOG_FINALIZE();
    return kExitNg;
  }

  auto inspect_response = result.TakeOk().value();
  auto data_points = inspect_response.GetDataPoints();

  if (data_points.empty()) {
    YORIITO_LOG_ERROR("inspect", "Inspect failed: No data points returned.");
    YORIITO_LOG_FINALIZE();
    return kExitNg;
  }

  const auto &inspect_data = data_points.front();

  const auto &path = inspect_data.GetPath();
  // const auto &data_type = inspect_data.GetDataType();
  // const auto &entry_type = inspect_data.GetEntryType();
  // const auto &deprecation = inspect_data.GetDeprecation();
  // const auto &unit = inspect_data.GetUnit();
  // const auto &min = inspect_data.GetMin();
  // const auto &max = inspect_data.GetMax();
  // const auto &comment = inspect_data.GetComment();
  // const auto &allowed = inspect_data.GetAllowed();
  // const auto &default_value = inspect_data.GetDefaultValue();
  const auto &description = inspect_data.GetDescription();
  // const auto &array_size = inspect_data.GetArraySize();
  // const auto &pattern = inspect_data.GetPattern();
  // const auto &custom_attributes = inspect_data.GetCustomAttributes();

  YORIITO_LOG_INFO("inspect", "Inspect succeeded");
  YORIITO_LOG_INFO("inspect", std::string("Path: ") + path);
  YORIITO_LOG_INFO("inspect", std::string("Description: ") + description);

  YORIITO_LOG_FINALIZE();
  return kExitOk;
}

Build & run steps

  1. Start the simulator if it is not running yet.

    $ cd /work/ref_pal
$ npm ci
$ ./init_pal.sh
$ npx electron . --no-sandbox

  2. Build

    $ cd /work/tutorial/inspect
$ cmake -S . -B build
$ cmake --build build -j

  3. Run

    $ ./build/inspect

Example use cases

Inspect is mainly used in the following situations:

  • Check before sending operation requests
    • Confirm that the value to be set is within the min/max range of the signal.
  • GUI control
    • Display min/max values for temperature settings or window opening percentage.
    • Prevent users from setting values outside the valid range.
  • Support multiple vehicle types
    • Obtain the correct range even when controllable ranges differ across vehicle types and equipment.

docs.title: 5-3-3. Control the simulator vehicle via Text User Interface (TUI)
docs.text:
So far, you have learned the Yoriito Signal API through coding. VSS defines many more signals, and various applications can be developed using them.

Writing code each time just to check a signal's behavior is time-consuming. For this purpose, a Text User Interface is provided. For usage, see "Connect vshot" in the PAL developer tutorial.

docs.title: 5-4-1. "Tools or libraries not found" errors
docs.text:
• Cause You may be running commands in the host environment instead of inside the container.

  • Countermeasure

    • Start the container as described in "4-5. Start the container" and run commands in a terminal inside the container.
    • All required tools and libraries are already installed in the container.

docs.title: 5-4-2. "Cannot connect to localhost (127.0.0.1)" error
docs.text:
• Cause Even local communication (localhost / 127.0.0.1) may be routed through a proxy, which can prevent a proper connection to localhost.

  • Countermeasure

    • Check the proxy-related environment variables (no_proxy / NO_PROXY) in the container.

    • Running the following commands in the container terminal may resolve the issue:

      $ export no_proxy=127.0.0.1,localhost  
$ export NO_PROXY=127.0.0.1,localhost

    • If this resolves the issue, add remoteEnv to .devcontainer/devcontainer.json so that the setting persists after restarting the container. After changing the settings, rebuild the Dev Container.

      "remoteEnv": {
  "no_proxy": "127.0.0.1,localhost",
  "NO_PROXY": "127.0.0.1,localhost"
},

docs.title: 6-1. Introduction
docs.text: In the previous chapter, we looked at sample code that demonstrates how to use the Yoriito Signal API. In this chapter, we introduce a sample application that makes practical use of the Yoriito Signal API.

docs.title: 6-2. Understand the App Architecture
docs.text:
The overall architecture of the sample application is shown in the figure below.

GUI Application (Flutter)

  • This is the front‑end (screen) operated by the user, implemented with Flutter.
  • In this sample, the GUI Application and the Headless Application are separated into different processes so that the UI framework can be replaced more easily.
  • However, when using the API, neither Flutter nor this process separation is mandatory.
  • This architecture is presented simply as one example of how to develop a GUI Application using the Yoriito Signal API.
  • Target code: yoriito-tutorial/ref_ui

Headless Application (C++)

  • This is the back-end (non-GUI) application that acts as a BFF (Backend For Frontend), processing requests from the GUI Application.
  • It calls the Yoriito Signal API and communicates with the GUI Application via gRPC.
  • It is implemented in C++.
  • Target code: yoriito-tutorial/ref_app

Yoriito Signal API

  • This is the vehicle‑oriented API used from the Headless Application.
  • The API is provided as shared libraries named libyoriito_vehicle_api_<domain>.so.

Yoriito VISS Server

  • As a data broker, it relays vehicle signal information from PAL to applications, and forwards actuator control requests from applications to PAL.

PAL

  • This is the lowest layer, directly interfacing with the platform-dependent I/O and the physical vehicle.
  • In this tutorial, the 3D car model plays this role.
  • Target code: yoriito-tutorial/ref_pal

docs.title: 6-3. Understand the App Contents
docs.text: The sample application features an emergency button. When you press the emergency button in the app, windows and doors close, and lights turn on.

docs.text:

docs.title: 7. Developing a custom PAL to connect CAN and Kura 🚗
7-1. Introduction
docs.text:
This page explains how readers can develop their own PAL to connect CAN and Kura. This page assumes the following knowledge:

  • VSS/VISS

docs.title: 7-2-1. Clone the yoriito-tutorial repository
docs.text:
This tutorial uses sample PAL called pocket-pal. yoriito-tutorial repository contains pocket-pal, so at first, please clone yoriito-tutorial. pocket-pal is located in the pocket-pal directory. 

$ git clone https://github.com/yoriito/yoriito-tutorial.git

pocket-pal uses vcan device, so you need a vcan (Virtual CAN interface), so create it as follows: 

$ bash yoriito-tutorial/pocket-pal/script/setup_vcan.sh

This script performs the following operations, so you can also execute them manually: 

# load vcan module
$ sudo modprobe vcan
# create virtual CAN device (vcan0) as a network device
$ sudo ip link add dev vcan0 type vcan
# set status to `UP`
$ sudo ip link set up vcan0

docs.title: 7-2-2. Start the development Docker container
docs.text:
yoriito-tutorial provides a development Docker container for yoriito project. From the root of yoriito-tutorial repository, launch VS Code and start the development Docker container for the pocket-pal directory by following the steps described there.

When you run shell commands in the following location in VS Code, they will be executed inside the development Docker container.

Warning

⚠️ Unless otherwise noted, the following assumptions apply to subsequent code blocks:

  • Commands are executed inside this development container.
  • The current directory is /work/pocket-pal in the cloned repository.

docs.title: 7-3-1. Design of pocket-pal-cc
docs.text:
Before staring your custom PAL, let's take a look at the design of pocket-pal-cc. pocket-pal-cc consists of three C++ source files and CMakeLists.txt as follows. 

$ tree -L 1 pocket-pal-cc 
pocket-pal-cc
├── build
├── can_broker.h
├── CMakeLists.txt
├── main.cpp
└── vss_broker.h
2 directories, 4 files

Their responsibilities are as follows.

file responsibility main.cpp - Implements the entry point of pocket-pal - Receives CAN from vcan, converts it to VSS, and writes it to Kura - Receives VSS from Kura, converts it to CAN, and writes it to vcan - Manages the threads that execute the above functions can_broker.h - Provides write functions to vcan - Provides read functions from vcan vss_broker.h - Provides write functions to Kura - Provides subscribe functions for specific VSS data in Kura CMakeLists.txt - Describes CMake configuration for pocket-pal-cc - Adds header search paths - Links libraries build - Working directory for building

docs.title: 7-3-2. Build and run pocket-pal-cc
docs.text:
Now you understand how pocket-pal-cc works, let's build and run it. You can build and run it with the following steps: 

# Build
$ mkdir pocket-pal-cc/build && cd pocket-pal-cc/build
$ cmake ..
$ make
# Run
$ ./pocket-pal

This sample pal runs in a loop, reading CAN frames from vcan, converting them to VSS, and writing them to Kura. For more details, see the following diagram.

docs.title: Modify CAN → VSS conversion
docs.text:
Here we modify the implementation that receives a CAN signal from vcan, converts it to VSS, and writes it to Kura. This process is implemented in the main.cpp(link). 

void on_can(std::shared_ptr<CANBroker> can_broker) {
  while (running) {
    auto frame = can_broker.get()->read();
    if (!frame.has_value()) {
      continue;
    }
    auto valid_frame = frame.value();
    YORIITO_LOG_INFO("CAN", "[RECV] id: " + std::to_string(valid_frame.can_id) +
                                ", data: " + format_can_data(valid_frame));

    VSSBroker::write<std::uint8_t>(WINDOW_POSITION, 100, true, true);
    YORIITO_LOG_INFO("VSS", "[SEND] path: " + std::string(WINDOW_POSITION) +
                                ", payload: 100");
  }
}

As shown above, the data received from vcan is stored in the variable valid_frame. The code writes the value 100 to Kura with the path WINDOW_POSITION (=Vehicle.Cabin.Door.Row1.DriverSide.Window.Position).

For example, if you want to modify the implementation so that when the received CAN ID is 0x100, the first byte of the CAN payload is treated as window position and written to Kura, it will look like this.

    }
    auto valid_frame = frame.value();
    YORIITO_LOG_INFO("CAN", "[RECV] id: " + std::to_string(valid_frame.can_id) +
                                ", data: " + format_can_data(valid_frame));

-   VSSBroker::write<std::uint8_t>(WINDOW_POSITION, 100, true, true);
-   YORIITO_LOG_INFO("VSS", "[SEND] path: " + std::string(WINDOW_POSITION) +
-                               ", payload: 100");
+   if (valid_frame.can_id == 0x100) {
+     auto position = static_cast<std::uint8_t>(valid_frame.data[0]);
+     VSSBroker::write<std::uint8_t>(WINDOW_POSITION, position, true, true);
+     YORIITO_LOG_INFO(
+         "VSS", "[SEND] path: " + std::string(WINDOW_POSITION) +
+                    ", payload: " +
+                    std::to_string(static_cast<unsigned int>(position)));
+   }

}

When you actually develop a PAL, you will update VSS data in Kura based on the received CAN frame in this way.

As shown in above link, the data received from Kura is stored in the variable data_point. The code writes a hard-coded payload to vcan with CAN ID 256.

docs.title: 7-4. Verify the Behavior
docs.text: This section explains how to verify the behavior by writing CAN data to pocket-pal-cc or writing VSS data and checking the result.

docs.title: 7-4-2. Write a CAN frame to vcan and verify that it is written to Kura as VSS
docs.text:
First, run pocket-pal-cc inside the development Docker container: 

$ ./pocket-pal-cc/build/pocket-pal

Then, follow these steps.

The detailed steps are as follows.

  1. Send a CAN frame Run the following command in a shell. You can run this either inside the development Docker container or on the host OS. 
    $ cansend vcan0 123#1122334455667788
  2. Send a VSS signal After step 1, PAL converts the received data to a VSS signal and notifies Kura.
  3. Read the VSS signal Use the TUI to get the value. If you have not modified pocket-pal, the path to get is Vehicle.Cabin.Door.Row1.DriverSide.Window.Position.
  4. Check the returned VSS signal The TUI returns the value of Vehicle.Cabin.Door.Row1.DriverSide.Window.Position. If you have not modified pocket-pal, you should get 100.

docs.title: 7-5-4. Cannot use vcan on WSL2
docs.text:
• Symptom 
    $ sudo modprobe vcan
modprobe: FATAL: Module vcan not found in directory /lib/modules/....
  • Cause The standard WSL2 kernel does not include the vcan module.
  • Countermeasure Resolve the issue by referring to the following information. Note that the location of configuration items may have changed. Within this project, the following procedure has been confirmed to work. 
    git clone --depth 1 -b linux-msft-wsl-6.6.y https://github.com/microsoft/WSL2-Linux-Kernel.git
cd ~/WSL2-Linux-Kernel
make mrproper
zcat /proc/config.gz > .config
printf "CONFIG_CAN=m\nCONFIG_CAN_RAW=m\nCONFIG_CAN_BCM=m\nCONFIG_CAN_GW=m\nCONFIG_CAN_DEV=m\nCONFIG_CAN_VCAN=m\n" >> .config
make olddefconfig
make modules -j$(nproc)
sudo make modules_install

docs.title: 8. Glossary
docs.text: word definition Yoriito Vehicle API An API standardization activity by the Yoriito project to abstract access to vehicle signals, composed of Yoriito Signal API and Yoriito Access API. Yoriito Project Open source project that provides Yoriito Vehicle API and related components, defining the scope and architecture for vehicle signal access. Access API High-level API that abstracts  Signal API for specific use cases, focusing on usability for applications. Access Library Shared library that implements the  Access API for applications. Signal API Low-level application-facing API that provides access to vehicle signals based on  VSS definitions. Signal Library Shared library implementation of the  Signal API for applications. VISS Extended VISS protocol and message schema set tailored for  Vehicle API for accessing vehicle signals. VISS Server Central data broker server that manages the VSS data tree and mediates communication between applications and PAL. VISS Consumer Library Client library for applications to access  VISS Server using the VISS protocol. VISS Producer Library Client library for PAL implementations to supply signals and receive actuator targets from  VISS Server. VSS Extended VSS signal definitions provided by  for OEMs and suppliers to derive vehicle-specific VSS trees. devcontainer Pre-configured development container environment including SDKs and toolchains for  Vehicle API. Vehicle API platform Platform composed of multiple  components, versioned as a whole release unit. Capability Concept representing whether a feature or equipment physically exists and is provided by the vehicle. Availability Concept representing whether a feature is currently usable under given vehicle conditions, expressed as boolean. Signal API error vocabulary Common error vocabulary shared across components to unify error handling for  Vehicle API. Inspect API method to retrieve metadata such as type, unit, and range for a given signal path. Headless App Backend C++ application that receives UI requests via gRPC and calls  Signal API. Platform Abstraction Layer Abstraction layer between vehicle platform and  VISS Server, converting platform-specific signals to VSS. TUI (Text User Interface) Text-based UI provided to operate simulator vehicle and test various signals without coding.
